projects.name: 1.1.2.15 - Capacity Building for Environmentally Sound PCBs Management and Disposal
projects.description:
The project will enable environmentally sound management (ESM) and disposal of targeted PCB containing oil and equipment in fulfillment of Mongolia’s commitments under the Stockholm Convention. The project will develop regulatory infrastructure and strengthen national capacity toidentify, monitor, manage, and treat PCBs in an environmentally sound manner as required by the Convention. Strengthened capacity for ESM of PCBs will include both discarded equipment and equipment remaining in use, so that continued operation of that equipment does not constitute a global environmental risk until it is retired as provide for by the Stockholm Convention. In accordance with the Basel and Stockholm Conventions guidelines, the project will also directly provide for treatment of a minimum of 1,000 tons of identified targeted PCBs, including PCB-containing equipment and oil.
The overall objective was to create capacity for environmentally sound management of PCBs for preventing PCBs releases from the electric equipment, avoiding cross-contamination of electric equipment and disposing of 1,000 tons of PCBs wastes. The positive impact for the project meant to reduce the risks of PCBs releases to the environment to prevent the subsequent negative effects on humans and on the environment. In terms of this indicator of impact, the project contributed to the successful treatment of 1,002 tons of PCB.

projects.name: 1.1.1.17 - IOM Project "Understanding and Managing Internal Migration in Mongolia"
projects.description:
Mongolia has experienced massive rural-to-urban migration to the capital city Ulaanbaatar (UB). Largely as a result of these arrivals, 48% of 3.2 million population lives in Ulaanbaatar. The majority of urban migrants are economically active people aged 25-39 years whose reasons for migration are search for employment, better living conditions and greater access to services.
Most urban migrants reside in the ger areas of UB where access to services is insufficient and inadequate, and where air pollution levels are highest. Additionally, lack of adequate information, access to decent work, and migration restriction pose significant challenges. projects.name: 3.1.1.10 - IOM Project Strengthening Mongolia's efforts to prevent and respond to human trafficking
projects.description:
Mongolia is a source and destination country for men, women and children subjected to trafficking in persons for the purpose of forced labour and sexual exploitation. Human trafficking within Mongolian borders is also a problem with thousands of women and children estimated to be trafficked every year from rural communities into cities and/or abroad . 
To help the Government of Mongolia (GoM) consistently identify and protect victims, the project will introduce a set of mutually reinforcing activities centred on communication and outreach, migrant empowerment, data collection and information sharing, capacity building trainings for government officials and stakeholders, and victim direct and reintegration assistance.
The prevention component of the project will include targeted activities that will move beyond awareness-raising to effecting positive behavior change through understanding the risks of human trafficking associated with migration decisions and improving knowledge of how to practice informed migration. Beneficiaries of awareness raising activities will primarily include young women and girls in rural areas, ger districts of Ulaanbaatar and mining and border areas. The proposed project will also contribute to eliminating and preventing exploitation and human trafficking by better guiding and providing private sector partners with practical guidelines and solutions for the implementation of ethical recruitment. This will be achieved through a training on ethical recruitment training for selected Private Recruitment Agencies (PRAs) and availability of a self-assessment tool to review the recruitment practices. The project will also target vulnerable prospective migrant workers (both male and female) who endeavor to travel abroad for work, through customization of IOM's MigApp , a user friendly, one-stop-shop mobile application to access readily available information and services relevant to their specific migration process.
In line with the government National Anti-Trafficking Program (NAP 2017-2021) aimed at improving prevention and protection, the project will engage with education and academic centers to empower learners to engage in society as constructive and ethically responsible agents of change, supporting justice and strong institutions. Awareness trainings will be held for 100 high school and university teachers and educators in Ulaanbaatar city, as well as Counter-Trafficking School forums for up to 1,000 students. 
Under the protection component, IOM will further support the government in its counter-trafficking efforts through a comprehensive baseline assessment into the underlying causes, dynamics, vulnerability and resilience levels to trafficking in Mongolia, as envisaged in NAP 2017-2021. The study will result in policy and programme recommendations for the government and NGOs. Research results will also inform the participatory development of materials necessary for awareness-raising, capacity building workshops for law enforcement and other frontlines officers working at Mongolian borders and major Chinese airports, as well as future policy directions of the Government of Mongolia, to respond to capacity building needs of law enforcement and other frontline officers, considering TIP patterns from/to Mongolia through Chinese main air transit hubs. These protection efforts will include development of e-training module for Consular Officials on victim identification and protection.
To address the urgent need to improve assistance and protection of trafficked persons , the project will aim to improve victims’ assistance and increase their chances for successful (re)integration into society. This will be done through improved collaboration with Anti-Human Trafficking Network of NGOs, introduction of life skills trainings for Victims of Trafficking (VoTs) in addition to direct and reintegration assistance, as well as capacity building trainings to One Stop Center workers in 20 provinces and Ulaanbaatar city to identify and protect victims.

The objective of the project is to strengthen the Government of Mongolia's capacity to prevent trafficking in persons and protect victims within Mongolia and abroad. To achieve its objective, the project is expected to produce outcomes under two project components: 1. Government and civil society coordinate effectively to identify victims of trafficking; 2. GoM consistently identifies and protects victims in line with international standards and best practices.

projects.name: 1.1.2.25 - UNEP OzonAction Programme
projects.description:
Mongolia is a Party to the Vienna Convention and the Montreal Protocol for the protection of the ozone layer from ozone depleting substances (ODS). Mongolia’s National Hydrochloroflurocarbon (HCFC) Phase-Out Management Plan (HPMP) Stage-I, approved at the 63rd Meeting of the Executive Committee (ExCom) of the Multilateral Fund in 2011, aims to reduce HCFC consumption by 35 per cent from the baseline value of 1.4 Ozone Depleting Potential (ODP) tonnes by 2020. The country has completed implementing the HPMP stage I, third tranche in December 2020 and currently implementing the last and fourth tranche of stage I, which was approved based on the inter-sessional approval process as part of 85th Meeting of the ExCom in 2020. The HPMP stage I is expected to be completed in December 2020.
Also, the HPMP Stage II for Mongolia was approved based on the inter-sessional approval process as part of 86th Meeting of the ExCom for the period from 2020 to 2030 for the complete phase-out of HCFC consumption by 2030. The country will implement the first tranche of the HPMP stage II until December 2023.
The projects are being implemented with UNEP as the lead implementing agency and Government of Japan as the cooperating agency. Some of the main activities undertaken are strengthening of HCFC control policies and regulations, capacity building of customs and refrigeration and air-conditioning servicing sector, procuring refrigerant identifiers for customs, awareness raising and project management and coordination. 

The Multilateral Fund adopted decision 79/46 related to enabling activities for Article 5 countries. The decision provides funding support to Article 5 parties to initiate activities that would facilitate their early ratification of the Kigali Amendment and undertake activities that help them fulfil their initial obligations with regard to hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) phase-down in line with the Kigali Amendment. At the 80th Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Multilateral Fund, the Enabling Activities for Kigali Amendment for Mongolia was approved with UN Environment as the implementing agency. The project has been implemented from November 2017 till December 2020 and successfully completed. UNEP and the Government of Mongolia will submit the project completion report in 2021. The main activities of the project were: assessment of the market, national policy framework, licensing & quota system, refrigeration servicing sector needs and awareness raising for Kigali Amendment.

The 83rd Executive Meeting of the Multilateral Fund approved the institutional strengthening (IS) project Phase XI to continue strengthening the functioning of the Mongolian National Ozone Unit for successful coordination, monitoring and implementation of the Montreal Protocol projects in the country.

projects.name: 1.1.1.31 - Developing Capacities for the Production of Radioisotopes
projects.description: According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2012 report data, Mongolia has the highest cancer mortality rate in the world, recording an estimated 161 deaths per 100 000 population. In 2012, there were about 3121 cancer deaths, and it is expected that this number will reach 7037 by 2035. Several national plans and strategies have been put in place to provide better services to patients, but there are a few limiting factors in providing cancer diagnosis and treatment to all patients. Currently, there is only one gamma camera in operation with full capacity, thereby seriously limiting the number of patients who can receive service. By 2025, it is expected that a total of eight gamma cameras will be installed, to be located in the Western region (regional health centre), Eastern region (regional health centre), and rest in Ulaanbaatar, namely in the First State Hospital, Second General Hospital and National Cancer Centre. Major radioisotopes required are technetium-99m, iodine-131 and iodine-125. The current demand of technetium-99m generators is 12 Ci per year, which is for only one gamma camera. All isotopes are imported, Mongolia does not produce any radioisotopes domestically. By 2025, the demand of radioisotopes, especially technetium-99m, is expected to reach about 100 Ci per year (2-3 Ci per week). The reliable supply for the technetium-99m generator is an important issue. Transportation cost and unforeseen delays in delivery are major considerations. For addressing these issues, there is a need for producing/dispensing a technetium-99m generator in Mongolia from imported molybdenum-99 (fission Molly). By doing so, supply and transportation will become much easier and reliable. Capacity building and human resource development is the first step for achieving this goal.

projects.description: The successful implementation of this project will contribute towards national efforts to respond to the growing demand for radiotherapy in the country with the latest techniques and quality in line with international best practices and standards. Cancer prevention and control in Mongolia is being implemented under the framework of the National Programme on Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases 2017–2021. In the field of radiotherapy, the programme focuses on (1) installing linear accelerators (LINACs); (2) upgrading teletherapy to four dimensional technology, and brachytherapy to three dimensional technology; and (3) improving radiotherapy quality assurance and radiation protection to comply with international standards. These objectives are aligned with the Strategic Plan to Develop Radiotherapy in Mongolia 2011–2021 which aims to introduce advanced technologies such as three dimensional (3-D) conformal radiation therapy (3DCRT), intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), image guided radiation therapy (IGRT), volumetric intensity modulated arc therapy (VIMAT), and stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in a phased manner. The introduction of LINAC based advanced techniques in this project requires addressing three key areas, namely (1) installing advanced equipment for radiotherapy with respiratory gating; (2) improving personnel knowledge and skills in the field of radiotherapy advanced techniques; and (3) developing treatment protocols for respiratory gating. By introducing advanced equipment and technologies for respiratory gating, accuracy of treatment planning will be improved. This will require use of infrared cameras and upgraded treatment planning system software. Treatment protocols will be developed, and workflows will be standardized, resulting in better target delineation and identification of organs at risk, especially those that are moving. Improving personnel knowledge and professional skills in advanced technologies will result in fewer side effects and better tumour control, leading to better treatment outcomes. Hence, quality of life and survival of patients will be enhanced.

projects.name: 1.1.1.33 - Improving Treatment Outcomes through the Introduction of Image-Guided 3-D Brachytherapy Technique
projects.description: There is an increasing trend in the incidence of cancer in Mongolia over the last few years. For instance, in 2005, the number of newly diagnosed cancer cases was 132.9 per 100 000 population, but it increased to 186.0 in 2013. Cervical cancer is the second leading cancer for women and oesophageal cancer is fourth for both men and women. Most of them are diagnosed in late stages, when radiotherapy is an important treatment option. Supported by the hospital registration data, there are a large number of cancer cases requiring Brachytherapy treatment in Mongolia. Over 200 cervical cancer patients receive Brachytherapy and about 800 applications are performed each year. Currently, we are performing X ray-based two-dimensional (2-D) Brachytherapy treatment planning, and several reference points have been used as the standard dose-specific points (e.g. points A/B, rectal/bladder reference points defined by the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements in intra-cavitary Brachytherapy for cervical cancer). However, the treatment planning based on reference points identified in the 2-D treatment plan is not the optimal treatment planning method, when aiming for the most desirable treatment outcomes and avoiding complications in normal organs. Recently, 3-D images acquired by computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have increasingly been used for treatment planning of Brachytherapy, as these imaging modalities provide more accurate information than X rays when it comes to the spatial relationship of the radioactive sources, tumours, and organs at risk (OARs). Treatment planning using 3-D images also allows for better quality assessment of the treatment using tools such as 3-D dose distributions and dose-volume evaluation for tumours and OARs, and thus leads to optimized treatment for the individual. Therefore, introduction of image guided 3-D Brachytherapy will further improve the treatment outcomes. This requirement to introduce 3-D IGBT is stated in VI.1.3 of "Country Programme Framework in 2016-2021". A GyneSource high dose rate (HDR) Brachytherapy machine (Bebig) has been operational since 2009. Source replacement in the near future must be considered since the current Cobalt source is nearing its half-life and the treatment time is long. This can result in the patient moving during treatment - hence the applicator/s position may shift during treatment. Human capacity building is another significant issue for consideration. Radiation oncologists, medical physicists and radiation therapy technologists (RTTs) have been trained in various training courses through fellowships. They are capable of introducing this new technique with further training. Several of our specialists participated in the training course of the IAEA regional project RAS6062 and gained knowledge about 3-D IGBT. To introduce this advanced Brachytherapy technique in the country, it is compulsory to train specialized professionals in developed countries for a longer period. It is also crucial to invite IAEA experts in Brachytherapy to learn, work together and solve problems in the workplace. Overall, this project is aimed to improve Brachytherapy quality assurance by upgrading existing Brachytherapy software, purchasing some CT/MRI compatible applicators, replacing old Co-60 source of “Gynesource” afterloading unit and human capacity building.

Notwithstanding these constraints, there is urgent demand for IRC to already commence preparatory work for the priority projects and the Trilateral Investment Projection Center. projects.name: Aligning the financial system and infrastructure investments with sustainable development - a transformational approach
projects.description: Given infrastructure’s cross-cutting relevance to the SDGs, as well as the complex, networked properties of infrastructure systems themselves, an integrated approach to infrastructure planning and development is crucial. Such an approach considers the interlinkages between different infrastructure systems, sectors, project phases, locations, and aspects of sustainability (environmental, social, and economic). Institutions and governance mechanisms that support multi-disciplinary cooperation and coordination across various policy levels (sub-national, national, international). Applying such an approach requires consultation with a broad array of stakeholders, and the institutions and governance mechanisms that support multi-disciplinary cooperation and coordination across various policy levels and ministries. This project aims to help Mongolian policymakers to apply such a “system-of-systems” approach to better assess the impacts of planned infrastructure upon the environment, to optimize trade-offs, identify synergies for more efficient operation, and to guard against lock-in of unsustainable practices. Specifically, this project focuses on large-scale and potentially transformational infrastructure investments and involved the mapping of major infrastructure development projects that impact Mongolia, overlaid against critical biodiversity zones and threatened habitat; areas at critical risk of land degradation, desertification, coastal erosion and deforestation; and other criteria relevant to three Multilateral Environmental Agreements (MEAs): the UNFCCC, the UNCCD and the UNCBD. The project estimates how the mapped infrastructure investments impact the environment in terms of the objectives of each of the MEAs and use modelling to compare the results of different infrastructure planning and investment scenarios. The global impact assessment and modelling methodology that was developed for use at the global scale will be adapted and applied at the country-level in Mongolia.

projects.name: 1.1.1.46 - UNIDO: Strategic cooperation framework between UNIDO and the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Light Industry of Mongolia 2021-2025
projects.description:
Director General’s approval-in-principle to develop a Strategic Cooperation Framework (SCF) for 20212-2025, between  UNIDO and MOFALI came in response to the letter of the Minister of MOFALI, dated 1 July 2021, inviting UNIDO to consider the formulation of the SCF (see Annex 1). The Framework recognizes the cooperation between UNIDO and MoFALI since Mongolia become a UNIDO Member State in 1985, and the fruitful cooperation carried out since then in the fields of sustainable food, agriculture and light industrial development, which has made a positive contribution to Mongolia's sustainable development, particularly with regard to the industrial sector. The Framework recognizes the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development adopted at the United Nations Summit in 2015, the Lima Declaration adopted at the fifteenth session of the UNIDO General Conference in 2013, as well as the Abu Dhabi Declaration adopted at the eighteenth session of the UNIDO General Conference in 2019 that welcomes UNIDO’s role in accelerating the achievement of SDG 9 along with all other industry-related goals of the 2030 Agenda with a primary objective to promote inclusive and sustainable industrial development (ISID) in its Member States.
The main objective of the Strategic Cooperation Framework (SCF) is to further strengthen the cooperation between MoFALI and UNIDO in the field of inclusive and sustainable industrial development (ISID) to advance the country’s capabilities in the food, agriculture and light industrial sectors. The SCF will define the broad areas of cooperation, based on UNIDO’s comparative advantages and Mongolia’s development priorities. The SCF is also expected to facilitate collaboration towards ISID, while contributing to the achievement of the SDGs and addressing issues of global concern, such as climate change and recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, this Strategic Cooperation Framework (20212-2025) establishes priorities on which MoFALI and UNIDO agree to focus, and contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), using UNIDO’s four main enabling functions of technical cooperation analytical and research functions and policy advisory services, normative functions and standards and quality-related activities, as well as convening and partnerships for knowledge transfer, networking and industrial cooperation.
